title: When Words Kill: How Institutions Govern a World That No Longer Exists
author: Greg O'Keefe
summary: Greg O'Keefe opens with the Boeing 737 MAX crashes — where 346 people died because Boeing certified a fundamentally new aircraft using the language and standards developed for a fifty-year-old design — and extends the analysis to a general theory of institutional language failure. The core argument is that every institution eventually develops governance language — safety standards, compliance frameworks, policy definitions, professional norms — calibrated to a world that existed at the time of the language's creation. When the world changes faster than the language, institutions continue applying the old words to new realities, producing invisible but potentially catastrophic mismatches between what the governance language says and what the governed phenomenon actually is. O'Keefe argues this is the defining institutional failure mode of the current AI transition: legal frameworks written for information scarcity now govern information abundance, educational standards designed for industrial-era knowledge demands now certify graduates for a world that has moved past those demands, and professional licensure built around human-only expertise now applies to AI-augmented practice in ways the licensing language cannot accurately assess. The article closes with a challenge to institutional leaders: the question is not whether your governance language is legally valid but whether it accurately describes the thing it is governing — and if it does not, the institution is operating the way Boeing operated, certain of its compliance while the world beneath it has changed.
points: The Boeing 737 MAX crashes are the article's most important case: Boeing's governance language said the plane was a variant of a fifty-year-old design; the actual aircraft was fundamentally different; people died not because Boeing violated its standards but because its standards had stopped describing the reality they governed.

The pattern generalizes: every institution's governance language is calibrated to a world that existed when the language was written, and the gap between the language and the current world is invisible from inside the institution because the institution is using the language to assess its own compliance.

The AI transition is the current instance of this failure mode: legal frameworks, educational standards, professional licensing, and institutional policies written before AI are now being applied to AI-transformed realities, producing the same structural mismatch that produced the Boeing crashes — technically compliant, substantively wrong.

The leadership challenge O'Keefe identifies is the hardest kind: institutions are structurally rewarded for compliance with their own language and structurally punished for challenging it, which means the institutions most at risk are the ones whose leaders are most confident they are doing things right.

The practical question for institutional leaders is not 'are we compliant?' but 'does our governance language accurately describe what we are actually governing?' — a question that requires looking outside the institution's own framework, which is precisely what the institutional incentive structure makes most difficult.
quotes: In October 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 crashed into the Java Sea twelve minutes after takeoff. Five months later, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 went down under almost identical circumstances.

This is not a story about negligence or fraud, though those questions have been litigated elsewhere. It is a story about something more structural, and in some ways more disturbing: the way institutional language can become decoupled from the reality it purports to govern, invisibly, gradually, and with catastrophic consequences.

That inheritance has real advantages: stable language is enforceable, legally defensible, professionally coherent. Those advantages create genuine resistance to revision, even when revision is obviously needed.

But the signals reinforcing stable language are dense and immediate, every successful certification milestone, every training classification that holds, while the signals that would motivate revision are diffuse, delayed, and filtered before they reach anyone with authority to act. Boeing’s oversight was almost entirely conducted after certification, not before.

When reality reasserted itself, $1.9 trillion in mortgage-backed securities were downgraded in a matter of months. The post-crisis fix was revealing: regulators introduced a new suffix, “(sf),” to distinguish structured finance ratings from corporate ones.

The words available to them encoded assumptions about authorship and misconduct that generative AI had rendered structurally inapplicable, and because those words were canonical, professionally reproduced, and legally embedded, they persisted. Why This Matters ISD is not an argument that institutions are stupid or corrupt.
That’s why it looks like a crash, a crisis, a cliff, rather than a gradual recalibration. By the time the gap between language and reality is undeniable, the gap is enormous.
